screens.title: Particle Systems for Visual Effects
screens.subtitle: Using Unity's Shuriken system to design expressive, efficient VFX

narration.text: Visual effects make actions feel real and memorable in a game. In this chapter you'll learn the core parts of Unity's Shuriken Particle System, how to combine modules to build explosions, smoke, fire and magical spells, and how to keep those effects efficient for real platforms. We'll explore the Main, Emission, Shape, Color over Lifetime, and Size over Lifetime modules, and look at renderer, collision, lights and trails too. I'll show concrete inspector settings for a one-shot explosion and a looping smoke effect, and then we'll move into scripting patterns for triggering and reusing particle systems at runtime. Throughout, you'll learn common performance pitfalls — overdraw, too many particles, and expensive materials — and practical fixes like lowering Max Particles, sharing materials for batching, and using object pooling. By the end you will be able to assemble a working explosion prefab, trigger it with a small C# script, and reason about trade-offs so your VFX enhance gameplay rather than hurt it. Think about an in-game explosion: the feel, timing and visibility matter more than raw particle count. How will you make an explosion feel heavy without killing frame rate?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Shuriken organizes particle behavior into focused modules. Mastering a few key modules and simple optimizations yields expressive and performant VFX.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Outcomes you will demonstrate after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will have four practical, demonstrable skills. First, you will be able to identify and configure core Shuriken modules such as Main, Emission, Shape, Color over Lifetime and Size over Lifetime, and explain how each affects particle motion and appearance. For example, you'll set a short duration and a burst for a one-shot explosion and looping rate for smoke. Second, you will create and tune common effects—explosion, smoke and simple fire—using module values and material choices so the effect fits the game style. Third, you will implement script-based control: instantiate or play a particle system from a C# component, and manage lifecycle so one-shot effects don't run forever. You will practice the sample ExplosionTrigger pattern that instantiates and destroys the prefab after its main duration. Fourth, you will apply basic optimization strategies: reduce Max Particles, minimize overdraw with small textures, reuse materials for batching, and use object pooling to avoid frequent instantiation. Each skill is practical: you'll build a prefab, trigger it in scene, and test performance to confirm the effect meets target frame rates. Which objective will you try first in the lab?

screens.title: What is a Particle System?
screens.subtitle: Definition, components and the illusion of complex phenomena

narration.text: A particle system is a collection of many small sprites or meshes that together create the appearance of complex visual phenomena such as smoke, fire, or explosions. Each element is a particle with a short life: it is emitted, moves, changes, and dies. The Shuriken Particle System in Unity exposes focused modules to control groups of related properties. The Main module holds the fundamental settings: Duration sets how long the system runs; Looping determines whether it repeats; Start Lifetime controls how long each particle exists; Start Speed sets initial velocity; Start Size and Start Color set initial appearance; Max Particles caps total active particles. Emission controls how many particles are produced and when, while Shape defines where they start. Other modules like Color over Lifetime and Size over Lifetime let particles evolve. For example, a puff of smoke is usually looping with a moderate Rate over Time combined with a Color over Lifetime gradient that fades alpha to zero. A one-shot explosion uses a short Duration and a Burst so many particles appear instantly then dissipate. A common misconception is to treat particle systems as single objects — instead, think of them as emergent groups where tweaking one module can change the entire feel. Practice: create a system and change Start Speed to see how movement immediately alters perceived weight. What single parameter will you tweak first to change an effect's personality?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Particle systems produce emergent visuals by emitting many short-lived particles whose properties are controlled by modular settings.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › What is a Particle System?
Concept

A particle system is a set of short-lived elements emitted over time that together create complex visual effects. Shuriken separates control into modules so you can tune emission, shape, lifetime, motion, and appearance independently.

Main
Duration, Looping, Start Lifetime, Start Speed, Max Particles
Emission
Rate over Time, Bursts
Shape
Sphere, Cone, Box, Edge
Color & Size
Color over Lifetime, Size over Lifetime
Example
Puff of smoke

Looping system, moderate Rate over Time, Color over Lifetime fades alpha to zero, Size over Lifetime grows slightly.

Why this matters

Understanding the modular structure lets you isolate changes: tweak the Shape to move emission origin without changing motion, or change Color over Lifetime to alter appearance without touching emission rates. That separation improves iteration speed and reuse.

  • Misconception: more particles always look better. Often fewer well-tuned particles deliver better clarity.
  • Misconception: particle systems don't need lifecycle management; one-shots can leak if not destroyed.
Key Takeaway

Think modularly: Main, Emission, Shape, Color, Size. Those five control most visual decisions.

screens.title: Main and Emission Modules
screens.subtitle: How fundamental settings and emission patterns shape effect timing

narration.text: Two of the first modules you will use are Main and Emission. The Main module sets the system's lifecycle and particle defaults: Duration, Looping, Start Lifetime, Start Speed, Start Size, Start Color and Max Particles. Duration and Looping decide whether the system repeats or runs once — use a short duration and no looping for explosions, a long looping duration for ambient effects like smoke. Start Lifetime controls how long each particle exists; pairing short lifetime with fast start speed makes quick, sharp bursts. Emission decides how particles are generated: Rate over Time creates steady streams like rain, while Bursts let you emit many particles instantly for explosions or muzzle flashes. For instance, configure Rate over Time to zero and add a Burst with 100 particles at Time 0 to make an explosion. A common pattern is to set Play On Awake off for one-shots, then instantiate and Play via script. Misconception: setting Max Particles very high is safe; in reality it allows more runtime cost. Always pick the smallest Max Particles that supports the visual. Example: if your explosion uses 100 particles per burst and can overlap twice in scene, set Max Particles to a bit above 200 to avoid clipping. Which emission pattern will your next effect use?

keyIdea.title: Timing & generation
keyIdea.text: Main controls defaults and lifecycle; Emission controls steady vs burst generation. Match them to whether the effect is continuous or a one-shot.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Main & Emission
Main module essentials

Main sets lifecycle and defaults. Duration and Looping control repetition. Start Lifetime and Start Speed shape motion. Max Particles caps runtime cost.

Duration
System runtime length; pair with Looping for continuous effects.
Max Particles
Limit active particles to control CPU/GPU work.
Concrete example
Explosion defaults

Duration 1.0, Looping off, Start Lifetime random between 0.5 and 1.0, Start Speed between 5 and 10, Max Particles 500.

Emission patterns

Rate over Time is steady emission. Bursts produce sudden groups. Combine them for layered effects.

Rate over Time
Good for smoke, rain, or flames.
Burst
Use a Time 0 burst for explosions or sparks.
Misconception

Many beginners leave Max Particles high. That lets extreme concurrent emission spike cost unexpectedly. Limit it conservatively.

Key Takeaway

Choose burst for one-shots, rate for continuous; set Max Particles to the minimum needed.

screens.title: Shape Module — Emission Volumes
screens.subtitle: Control where particles originate using shapes and offsets

narration.text: The Shape module determines the spatial volume or area from which particles are emitted. Common shapes include Sphere, Hemisphere, Cone, Box and Edge. Each shape has parameters you can tweak: a Cone uses angle and radius that influence spread; a Sphere uses radius for omnidirectional emission; a Box uses size for planar or volumetric sources. For example, set a Cone for a flamethrower effect to focus particles in a directional spread, or choose a Sphere for an omnidirectional explosion so particles radiate in all directions. You can also apply position offsets and align the shape to the emitter transform to match local geometry, like emitting smoke from a chimney opening. A practical tip is to start with a small radius for concentrated effects and increase it for softer, more diffuse starts. Misconception: shape only affects appearance; it also interacts with velocity and collision. If your particles start inside geometry, collisions may fire immediately. Example scenario: use a small Sphere radius 0.1 for an explosion core and a secondary larger Sphere burst for a smoke puff after the blast. That layering yields natural visual progression. What shape would you choose to simulate sparks off a metal surface?

keyIdea.title: Emission origin
keyIdea.text: Shape defines the emission volume; matching shape to the physical source improves believability and interaction with collision.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Shape Module
Available shapes
  • Sphere — omnidirectional bursts like explosions
  • Cone — directional beams like fire or magic spells
  • Box — planar or volumetric emission sources
  • Edge — line sources for trails or laser-like effects
  • Hemisphere — half-sphere spreads for ground-originating effects
Example
Sparks from a surface

Use Edge or a Cone with a narrow angle and small start radius to keep sparks close to the surface and moving outward.

Practical tips
  1. Start with a small radius for concentrated effects; increase for softer starts.
  2. Align the shape transform to the source object to maintain consistency when moving the source.
  3. Combine multiple shapes for layered effects: a tight core and a wider secondary puff.
Misconception

Some assume Shape only affects visuals. It also controls initial collision placement and influences velocity patterns when particles spawn inside a volume.

Key Takeaway

Choose a shape that matches the physical source and layer shapes for richer effects.

screens.title: Color and Size over Lifetime
screens.subtitle: Animating particle appearance across its lifespan

narration.text: Color over Lifetime and Size over Lifetime are two modules you will use to animate particle appearance. Color over Lifetime uses a gradient to change color and alpha over each particle's life. Use the alpha channel to fade particles smoothly to transparent, which is essential for smoke and soft glows. For a fireball, a gradient that goes from bright orange to yellow and then to transparent gives a believable burn-out. Size over Lifetime uses a curve to change scale: you might start small, quickly expand, and then shrink before death for a pop-like explosion. Combining the two yields strong visual storytelling: color conveys temperature and fade, size conveys energy release. A common mistake is relying solely on Start Color and Start Size; you lose dynamic evolution. Example: make a smoke puff that starts small, grows while losing opacity, then drifts away. Also remember that aggressive size increases can create overdraw if many particles overlap. Test with Max Particles reduced to see the visual at lower counts. As a quick exercise, set a particle to double in size halfway through its life and fade alpha to zero at the end to see the effect's perceived scale change. How will you use the gradient to communicate energy in your next effect?

keyIdea.title: Appearance over time
keyIdea.text: Use Color and Size over Lifetime to create natural fades, growth, and energy progression for particles.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Color & Size over Lifetime
Color over Lifetime

Define a color gradient that maps the particle life from birth to death. Use alpha to fade out particles smoothly to avoid hard pop-out.

Example gradient
Opaque orange → yellow → transparent
Tip
Small alpha at end reduces visible overdraw.
Size over Lifetime

Define a scale curve to grow, shrink, or pulse particles. A rapid grow then slow shrink works well for explosions; steady growth suits smoke.

Example curve
0.2 → 1.4 → 0.8 across life for a pop-and-settle effect.
Misconception

Relying only on start size and color makes effects static. Use over-lifetime modules to add motion and storytelling.

Key Takeaway

Over-lifetime modules add evolving behavior and make fewer particles look richer.

screens.title: Renderer, Materials and Render Modes
screens.subtitle: How render choices affect look and performance

narration.text: The Renderer module decides how particles are drawn. Render Mode options include Billboard, Stretched Billboard, Horizontal Billboard, Vertical Billboard, and Mesh. Billboard is the common default: particles always face the camera, which is inexpensive and great for soft sprites. Stretched Billboard stretches sprites along velocity, useful for fast-moving streaks like lasers or rain splashes. Mesh render mode lets you render full geometry per particle, which can look great but is significantly more expensive. The Renderer also assigns a Material, typically using a transparent shader and a soft circular or textured sprite atlas. A big performance trade-off is material complexity: multi-pass or heavy shaders increase G P U cost. Sharing the same material across multiple particle systems lets Unity batch draws and reduce overhead. Overdraw is another major cost: many overlapping transparent particles cause the G P U to shade the same screen pixels multiple times. To reduce it, use smaller particles, tighter size over lifetime, and avoid large screens of overlapping alpha-heavy sprites. Misconception: higher-resolution textures always look better; often a small soft texture scaled and tinted produces a cleaner, cheaper result. Example: replace a high-res smoke texture with a 64x64 soft circle and a gradient to reduce overdraw while preserving readability. What render mode will you pick for fast sparks?

keyIdea.title: Render trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Billboard modes are cheap and flexible; mesh and complex materials cost more. Share materials to enable batching and reduce draw calls.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Renderer & Materials
Render modes overview
Billboard
Always faces camera, good default for sprites.
Stretched Billboard
Stretches along velocity for streaks.
Mesh
Renders geometry per particle; higher quality, higher cost.
Horizontal/Vertical
Useful for effects that must sit on a plane or wall.
Example
Spark streaks

Use Stretched Billboard with a small texture and velocity-based stretch for visually clear sparks with low particle count.

Materials and overdraw

Prefer simple transparent shaders and small textures. Overdraw occurs when many transparent pixels overlap and increases GPU load dramatically.

  • Share materials across systems to enable batching and instancing.
  • Avoid multi-pass or costly fragment operations in particle materials.
  • Use atlases for sprite variation while keeping a single material.
Performance note

Test with reduced Max Particles to check visual fidelity at lower budgets and avoid overdraw hotspots.

screens.title: Collision, Lights and Trails Modules
screens.subtitle: Adding interaction, illumination, and motion trails

narration.text: Beyond core appearance and emission, Shuriken includes modules that enable interaction and extra visual richness: Collision, Lights and Trails. The Collision module allows particles to detect and react to scene geometry. Use it for sparks that bounce off a wall or debris that should stop on the ground. Keep in mind collision increases C P U cost — use it sparingly for visible, high-impact particles. The Lights module lets particles emit light; it's very effective for fire or magic but can be expensive if many particles produce lights. Typically enable Lights for a handful of particles or use a single light that follows the emitter for cheaper results. Trails create a persistent trailing mesh behind moving particles, excellent for meteors or energy blasts. Trails are generated by particles and produce additional rendering work; pair them with careful lifetime and quality settings. Example: enable Collision for a small set of bright sparks that interact with the player but leave smoke without collision. Common misconception: enabling every module makes an effect better. Instead, enable only modules that contribute clearly to the player's experience. Which module will you disable first if performance is tight?

keyIdea.title: Interaction & embellishment
keyIdea.text: Use Collision, Lights and Trails selectively for interaction and polish, balancing visual payoff against runtime cost.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Collision, Lights & Trails
Collision

Particles can collide with scene geometry. Useful for sparks and debris. Expect higher CPU cost; restrict to important particles.

Example
Sparks

Enable Collision for a small number of visible sparks so they bounce off surfaces and add realism.

Lights & Trails

Lights let particles illuminate nearby objects; use sparingly. Trails generate geometry behind moving particles for striking streaks.

  • Use a single light following the emitter as a cheaper approximation to many particle lights.
  • Limit trail length and resolution to reduce cost.
Design advice

Enable these modules only where the interaction or lighting creates meaningful player impact; otherwise keep them off to save performance.

screens.title: Optimization Strategies
screens.subtitle: Practical rules to reduce cost and keep VFX performant

narration.text: Optimization is critical for particle systems, especially on constrained platforms. There are several dependable strategies drawn from common problems. First, reduce Max Particles: fewer active particles directly reduce C P U and G P U work. Second, minimize overdraw by using compact, low-alpha textures and tighter size curves so particles overlap less. Third, culling: Unity will cull off-screen systems automatically, but check Renderer Culling Mode and disable expensive modules for distant systems. Fourth, batching: use a single material across many systems to enable G P U instancing and reduce draw calls. Fifth, pooling: avoid frequent Instantiate and Destroy for one-shot effects by reusing pre-warmed particle system GameObjects. For example, instead of instantiating an explosion prefab every click, pull from a pool of ready particle systems, position and Play them, then return them after they finish. A common mistake is ignoring materials: different materials break batching and cause extra draw calls. Example workflow: profile the scene, find the heaviest particle systems, reduce Max Particles in those systems first, then simplify materials, and finally implement pooling if instantiation is heavy. Which optimization will you try first in your project?

keyIdea.title: Optimization checklist
keyIdea.text: Limit Max Particles, reduce overdraw, share materials for batching, enable proper culling, and use object pooling for frequent spawns.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Optimization Strategies
Common strategies
  • Max Particles: trim to the minimum needed
  • Overdraw: use small soft textures and limit overlap
  • Culling: verify off-screen systems are culled
  • Batching: share materials to enable fewer draw calls
Pooling pattern

Pooling reuses GameObjects: pre-instantiate a pool of particle systems, enable and play them on demand, then disable and return to pool. This avoids allocation spikes and repeated destruction cost.

Example sequence
  1. Prewarm pool with N particle systems.
  2. On trigger, take one, set position, call Play.
  3. After main.duration, Stop and return to pool.
Performance focus

Always profile. Reduce particle counts before increasing texture resolution or adding per-particle lights.

screens.title: Scripting Particle Systems in C#
screens.subtitle: Play, Stop, instantiate and manage lifecycle via script

narration.text: Controlling particle systems from C# gives you precise timing and interaction. The common pattern is to hold a public ParticleSystem reference, position it, and call Play or Stop. For one-shot effects you often instantiate a prefab, Play, and Destroy after the main. duration to clean up. Avoid frequent Instantiate and Destroy in tight loops; prefer object pooling for frequently spawned effects. The example ExplosionTrigger pattern raycasts from the camera on mouse click, instantiates the prefab at the hit point, calls Play, then schedules Destroy using the particle system's main. duration. For looping effects, call Stop when you want to end emission. When scripting, avoid inspecting module fields every frame; cache references to ParticleSystem components and only call Play/Stop when state changes. Also remember that main. duration is on the main module: read newExplosion. main. duration to schedule cleanup. Misconception: calling Play repeatedly restarts emission but does not manage GameObject lifecycle. You must explicitly destroy or reuse the GameObject if it's a one-shot. Example: a pooled particle system is moved, played, and returned to the pool using a coroutine or a timed callback. Which approach—instantiation or pooling—fits your game's spawn rate?

keyIdea.title: Script control
keyIdea.text: Use Play and Stop for runtime control; prefer pooling over Instantiate/Destroy when spawn rate is high.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Scripting Particle Systems
Pattern overview

Common workflow: reference a ParticleSystem prefab, instantiate at position, call Play, and schedule destroy after main.duration. For looping systems, call Stop to halt emission.

Concrete snippet
// Instantiate prefab at hit point
ParticleSystem newExplosion = Instantiate(explosionPrefab, hit.point, Quaternion.identity);
newExplosion.Play();
Destroy(newExplosion.gameObject, newExplosion.main.duration + 0.1f);
Best practice

Cache references, avoid per-frame allocations, and prefer pooling for frequent spawns to prevent GC and instantiation spikes.

Pooling approach

Pre-instantiate a set of particle systems, disable them, then enable, position and Play on demand. After main.duration, disable and return to pool.

Why pool?
Reduces allocations and avoids repeated costly instantiate/destroy operations.
Lifecycle
Use a timed callback or coroutine using newExplosion.main.duration to return systems to the pool.
Key Takeaway

Scripted control is straightforward; pick pooling when spawn frequency is high to keep performance stable.

screens.title: Lab: Build an Explosion Effect
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step settings for a one-shot explosion prefab

narration.text: This hands-on lab guides you through creating an explosion effect and wiring it to an ExplosionTrigger script. Start by creating a new empty GameObject named ExplosionManager, then add a Particle System and name it ExplosionEffect. In the Main module set Duration to 1.0 and uncheck Looping so it acts as a one-shot. Configure Start Lifetime to Random Between Two Constants such as 0.5 and 1.0, Start Speed Random Between Two Constants like 5 and 10, and Start Size Random Between Two Constants like 0.5 and 1.5. Set Max Particles to 500. In Emission set Rate over Time to 0 and add a Burst at Time 0 with Count 100. In Shape choose Sphere with Radius 0.1 for a compact core. Enable Color over Lifetime and create a fiery gradient from opaque red to orange to yellow that fades to transparent. Enable Size over Lifetime and shape a curve that starts small, grows quickly, then shrinks slightly before end. In Renderer choose Billboard and assign a simple particle material with a soft circular texture. Important: uncheck Play On Awake. Finally, drag the ExplosionEffect into the Project window to make a prefab. These concrete settings produce a responsive explosion you can trigger via script. After making the prefab, test it in scene to validate timing and look. What tweak will you try if it feels too heavy on frame time?

keyIdea.title: Lab steps
keyIdea.text: Follow the Main, Emission, Shape, Color and Size settings to create a one-shot explosion and save it as a prefab with Play On Awake disabled.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Explosion Lab
Step-by-step
  1. Create ExplosionManager and an ExplosionEffect particle system.
  2. Main: Duration 1.0, Looping unchecked, Start Lifetime 0.5–1.0, Start Speed 5–10, Start Size 0.5–1.5, Max Particles 500.
  3. Emission: Rate over Time 0, add Burst Time 0 Count 100.
  4. Shape: Sphere, Radius 0.1.
  5. Color over Lifetime: fiery gradient to transparent. Size over Lifetime: quick grow then slight shrink.
  6. Renderer: Billboard, assign simple particle material. Uncheck Play On Awake.
  7. Make ExplosionEffect a prefab by dragging to Project.
Example inspector snippet
Main: Duration=1.0, Loop=false
Emission: Burst[0]=100
Shape: Sphere r=0.1
Color over Lifetime: red→orange→yellow→transparent
Size over Lifetime: 0.2→1.2→0.8
Checkpoints
  • Play On Awake is unchecked.
  • Prefab exists in Project window.
  • Effect plays correctly when instantiated and called Play.
Troubleshooting

If the effect is too heavy drop Max Particles and simplify the particle texture. If particles clip into geometry, slightly increase Shape radius or offset spawn position.

Key Takeaway

Concrete inspector values make it easy to reproduce an explosion that looks good and is manageable at runtime.

screens.title: Wiring the ExplosionTrigger Script
screens.subtitle: Raycast spawn and cleanup — connecting prefab to input

narration.text: Now that you have an ExplosionEffect prefab, connect it to input using a simple ExplosionTrigger script. The pattern uses a public ParticleSystem reference for the prefab. On left mouse click raycast from the camera to find the world hit point. When you hit geometry, instantiate the prefab at that position, call Play, and then destroy the instantiated GameObject after its main. duration to free resources. Important detail: read the duration from the instantiated system's main module to ensure timed cleanup matches the prefab settings. For frequently used explosions, replace Instantiate with a pooled Get and Release to avoid allocation spikes. Also consider parenting transient effects to a manager or leaving them unparented depending on world movement. Misconception: destroying immediately after Play may cut off trailing effects; use main. duration plus a small buffer. After wiring, test by clicking around the scene: explosions should appear at the hit point and be removed automatically. As a challenge, add a secondary smoke puff prefab that instantiates slightly after the explosion to simulate lingering smoke. How will you sequence the secondary effect timing? Wiring the ExplosionTrigger Script means raycast to spawn, instantiate and play the prefab, and destroy after main.duration. use pooling at scale.. In practical terms, raycast spawn and cleanup — connecting prefab to input. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Trigger pattern
keyIdea.text: Raycast to spawn, instantiate and Play the prefab, and Destroy after main.duration. Use pooling at scale.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › ExplosionTrigger
Starter pattern

On input, raycast to find a point in the world. Instantiate the ExplosionEffect prefab at that point, call Play, and Destroy the GameObject after the particle system's main.duration plus a small buffer.

Example snippet
ParticleSystem newExplosion = Instantiate(explosionPrefab, hit.point, Quaternion.identity);
newExplosion.Play();
Destroy(newExplosion.gameObject, newExplosion.main.duration + 0.1f);
Pooling note

If you spawn many explosions, pull from a pool and schedule return instead of destroying. This keeps allocations stable and reduces frame spikes.

Sequencing secondary effects

For a smoke puff after the blast, start a coroutine or use Invoke to instantiate the smoke prefab after a short delay, e.g., 0.2–0.4 seconds, and let it play its own lifecycle.

Avoid
Destroying the parent GameObject immediately if it contains trailing systems; use duration-based cleanup per system.
Key Takeaway

Match cleanup timing to each particle system's main.duration and use pooling when spawn rates are high.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
